papers.title: SEABench: Benchmarking Endogenous Misalignment In Self-Evolving Agents
papers.authors: Saswat Das, Parvati Viswanathan, Daniel Donnelly, Chang Huang, Sahar Abdelnabi, Ferdinando Fioretto
papers.abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents have gained prominence for their ability to improve after deployment by modifying their harness, including their controller instructions, memory management protocols, and reusable tools and skills, in response to user and environment feedback. However, locally useful updates may persist into later tasks where they produce unsafe behavior, even without direct adversarial influence. To study this risk, we introduce SEABench, a benchmark for studying endogenous misalignment arising from agent self-evolution, with 48 longitudinal task sequences that span multiple evolution surfaces, task domains, and harm types in a rich personal-assistant environment. To account for the stochasticity inherent in agentic operations, we provide an adaptive trajectory discovery pipeline that probes for failures while preserving original task intent and supports causal attribution through paired non-evolving agents and attribution scores. Our evaluation across multiple recent LLMs, evolution surfaces, and harm types reveals that self-evolution indeed increases task completion rates but often at the cost of safety failures that are absent for paired non-evolving baseline agents. We also show that qualitatively different safety behaviors emerge across evolution surfaces and harm types. Further, we show that this divergence in safety behavior is reflected in agents' chain-of-thought reasoning, which yields an effective monitoring strategy that can mitigate unsafe behavior with a low false positive rate.
takeaways: SEABench is a benchmark for endogenous misalignment in self-evolving LLM agents, using 48 longitudinal task sequences across multiple evolution surfaces, task domains, and harm types in a personal-assistant setting.

The paper introduces an adaptive trajectory discovery pipeline that probes failures while preserving task intent, and pairs evolving agents with non-evolving baselines plus attribution scores to support causal attribution.

Experiments show self-evolution can improve task completion but often triggers safety failures absent in baselines; the authors also find chain-of-thought differences can be used as a low-false-positive monitoring strategy to mitigate unsafe behavior.
actionItems: Review SEABench’s 48 longitudinal task sequences and the adaptive trajectory discovery pipeline to understand how endogenous misalignment is measured across evolution surfaces, task domains, and harm types.

Evaluate whether the chain-of-thought-based monitoring strategy reproduces the reported low false-positive mitigation effect on the benchmark’s self-evolving agents versus paired non-evolving baselines.
Ask whether the benchmark’s personal-assistant setting and reported safety failures are sufficient to justify adoption of self-evolving agents without additional safeguards in deployment.

papers.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
papers.authors: Chaoqian Ouyang, Ling Yue, Libin Zheng, Huanghui Guo, Shengxiang Xu, YiShu Wang, Ran Li, Jian Yin, Shaowu Pan, Shimin Di
papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cost representation for each execution segment, recording its own consumption and the context growth it introduces. Composing adjacent segments yields a cumulative estimate that captures the extra input cost incurred when context from earlier segments is re-read by every later call. As execution unfolds, newly observed evidence refreshes the forecast, requiring no additional LLM calls and incurring a mean cumulative prediction time of 32.8 ms per run on SWE-bench Verified. Across 4 task suites and 6 agent models, TokenCast's mean absolute error reduction against the strongest comparator averages 14.5% over 96 evaluated combinations. In offline budget-control replay, TokenCast uses 21.3% fewer tokens on average than a fixed-budget policy at matched trace completion. The code is available at https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/TokenCast.
takeaways: TokenCast learns a composable cost representation for LLM agent execution segments to forecast token consumption, including both segment cost and the context growth each segment introduces.

It is evaluated across 4 task suites and 6 agent models; forecasts are updated as runs unfold without extra LLM calls, with 32.8 ms mean cumulative prediction time per run on SWE-bench Verified and a 14.5% mean absolute error reduction over the strongest comparator across 96 combinations.
Practical implication: better online token budgeting for LLM agents, with offline budget-control replay showing 21.3% fewer tokens on average than a fixed-budget policy at matched trace completion.
actionItems: Review TokenCast’s composable cost representation and online forecast update mechanism to confirm how segment cost and context growth are encoded for each agent execution step.
Evaluate TokenCast against your own LLM agent traces by measuring prediction error and runtime overhead on multi-step tasks, comparing it to a fixed-budget policy or your current budget estimator.

Question whether the offline budget-control replay results and 32.8 ms per-run prediction cost are sufficient for your deployment constraints, given the paper’s low applicability signal and the need for accurate online budgeting.

papers.title: Reasoning with Continuous Latent Diffusion
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion generates complete reasoning solutions through iterative refinement in latent space. We introduce Latent Flow Reasoning Models (LFRMs), an ELF-based training and inference recipe. Our experiments show that accurate decoding alone does not ensure strong reasoning performance. We therefore learn compact representations from multiple layers of a strong autoregressive teacher. Their decomposition also enables asynchronous denoising at different rates. We show that prompt encodings need only preserve the information required for the correct text-conditional score, rather than exactly match teacher features, and use a staged curriculum to learn a compact prompt encoder that replaces the teacher Transformer at inference. We adapt DiffusionNFT to learned self-conditioning guidance and incorporate gold-solution endpoints to supplement sparse rewards. Our supervised models outperform reported results from recent continuous-diffusion baselines at comparable backbone scales on mathematical reasoning and HumanEval code generation. With a 638M-parameter denoising backbone and learned prompt conditioning, post-NFT LFRM-L achieves 63.74% pass@1 on GSM8K and 24.6% on MATH500 at 64 denoising steps, and 32.85% on HumanEval and 30.18% on HumanEval+ at 128 denoising steps. Code will be available at: https://github.com/chengxiang/LFRM
takeaways: Introduces Latent Flow Reasoning Models (LFRMs), an ELF-based continuous diffusion recipe for generating complete reasoning solutions in latent space, with compact prompt conditioning replacing the teacher Transformer at inference.

Uses compact representations distilled from multiple teacher layers, asynchronous denoising at different rates, staged prompt-encoder training, and DiffusionNFT adapted with learned self-conditioning guidance plus gold-solution endpoints to supplement sparse rewards.

Reports that decoding accuracy alone is insufficient for reasoning, and that LFRM-L outperforms recent continuous-diffusion baselines on GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, and HumanEval+ at comparable model scales, suggesting a practical path to stronger reasoning and code generation from continuous diffusion.
actionItems: Review the LFRM training/inference recipe details, especially compact prompt conditioning, asynchronous denoising, and the staged prompt-encoder curriculum, to map the method to your current reasoning pipeline.
Run a benchmark comparison against your existing reasoning and code-generation setup on GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, and HumanEval+ using comparable backbone scales and denoising step budgets.
Ask whether the inference cost and operational complexity of replacing the teacher Transformer with a learned prompt encoder and multi-rate denoising are acceptable for your deployment constraints.

papers.title: Simultaneous Translation between Sign Languages
papers.authors: Zetian Wu, Bowen Xie, Stefan Lee, Liang Huang
papers.abstract: Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) signers cannot converse in real time across different sign languages today: existing sign-to-sign translation systems run offline, requiring the full source clip before any target sign is emitted. Live use cases - e.g. broadcast interpretation and two-way video calls - instead demand simultaneous output, while the source signer is still signing. We present, to our knowledge, the first simultaneous sign-to-sign (S2S) translation system, with two wait-k regimes: test-time wait-k inference applied directly to a full-sentence model, and a trained wait-k model via stochastic multi-path supervision. We further introduce ca-Stream-AL, a computation-aware latency metric for streaming output. Averaged across six S2S directions on both a smaller human-verified test set and a larger synthetic S2S corpus, our streaming system achieves a 38% ca-Stream-AL reduction while staying within a 9% DTW-PA-MPJPE increase and a 2.1 BLEU-4 drop compared to the full-sentence baseline. A word-order case study probes how the streaming model handles word order mismatch between different sign languages - a consequence of simultaneous translation.
takeaways: Introduces the first simultaneous sign-to-sign translation system, enabling real-time output while the source signer is still signing.

Uses two wait-k approaches—test-time wait-k on a full-sentence model and a trained wait-k model with stochastic multi-path supervision—and adds ca-Stream-AL as a computation-aware streaming latency metric.

Reports averaged results across six translation directions and two test sets: 38% lower ca-Stream-AL with only a 9% DTW-PA-MPJPE increase and 2.1 BLEU-4 drop versus the full-sentence baseline, suggesting practical use for live interpretation and video calls.
actionItems: Review the two simultaneous sign-to-sign approaches described here—test-time wait-k on a full-sentence model versus a trained wait-k model with stochastic multi-path supervision—and compare how each affects streaming output quality and latency.

Evaluate the reported tradeoff by checking whether the 38% ca-Stream-AL reduction with a 9% DTW-PA-MPJPE increase and 2.1 BLEU-4 drop holds consistently across the six sign-language directions and both the human-verified and synthetic test sets.

Assess adoption risk by asking whether the reported streaming gains and ca-Stream-AL metric are sufficient for real-time broadcast interpretation and two-way video calls, given the offline-only baseline and the word-order mismatch case study.

papers.title: ScAn-Bench: Evaluating Scaling Analysis Methodology
papers.authors: Artin Sermaxhaj, Nastaran Alipour, Donat Sinani, Johannes Hog, Neeratyoy Mallik, Jenia Jitsev, Danny Stoll
papers.abstract: Recent progress in machine learning is driven by large-scale foundation models, where scaling laws and finding optimal scaling prescriptions for architecture, data, and hyperparameters are key in advancing the state-of-the-art. Therefore, it is surprising that no systematic study evaluates the methodology to obtain scaling laws and prescriptions across different model types. To shed light on this crucial blind spot and facilitate future research, we introduce the surrogate benchmarks ScAn-Bench-LLM and ScAn-Bench-VLM based on 4524 and 8024 checkpoints of language and vision-language model pipelines. On our benchmarks, we perform the first systematic evaluation of both data acquisition and extrapolation methodology for scaling analysis across different data modalities.
takeaways: Introduces ScAn-Bench-LLM and ScAn-Bench-VLM to study scaling-analysis methodology for language and vision-language foundation models.
Builds on 4,524 LLM checkpoints and 8,024 VLM checkpoints, then systematically evaluates data acquisition and extrapolation methods for scaling analysis across model types.
Provides a benchmarked way to assess scaling-law procedures, which can help researchers derive more reliable scaling prescriptions for architecture, data, and hyperparameters.
actionItems: Review ScAn-Bench-LLM and ScAn-Bench-VLM as benchmark datasets for assessing scaling-analysis methodology across language and vision-language model pipelines.
Run comparative experiments on the 4,524 LLM and 8,024 VLM checkpoints to evaluate data acquisition and extrapolation methods for scaling-law estimation.
Assess whether the benchmarked scaling-analysis procedures are practical to adopt reliably for deriving prescriptions for architecture, data, and hyperparameters.

papers.title: GPUPhysBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Correct and Efficient GPU Physics Simulation
papers.authors: Yuchen Sun, Jinjin He, Sinan Wang, Bo Zhu
papers.abstract: Writing fast GPU code for physical simulation is difficult: implementations must preserve numerical accuracy while handling irregular data access, synchronization, and iterative solvers. We introduce GPUPhysBench, a benchmark of 50 tasks testing whether coding agents can meet these demands. Tasks cover fluids, deformable solids, and granular materials, from individual simulation operators to complete simulators. Agents write, compile, test, and optimize GPU code with access to a NVIDIA GPU under fixed time budgets. We report pass rates and runtime performance relative to expert-optimized reference implementations. In a single-attempt evaluation of six frontier model-harness pairs, the two strongest pass all 50 tasks, but even the fastest reaches at least 0.9 the reference speed on only 22% of them, and no submission is more than 5% faster than the reference. The largest gaps arise in collision detection, constraint solving, and iterative solvers. GPUPhysBench brings physical simulation workloads to coding-agent evaluation, testing both the ability to implement numerical methods correctly and the ability to make them run efficiently.
takeaways: Introduces GPUPhysBench, a 50-task benchmark for coding agents on GPU physics simulation across fluids, deformable solids, and granular materials, spanning operators to full simulators.

Evaluates agents that write, compile, test, and optimize GPU code under fixed time budgets on an NVIDIA GPU; reports pass rates and runtime versus expert-optimized references, with the two strongest of six frontier model-harness pairs passing all 50 tasks in one-attempt evaluation.

Practical implication: the benchmark shows current agents can often be correct but still lag on efficiency, with the largest gaps in collision detection, constraint solving, and iterative solvers, motivating better methods for fast numerically accurate GPU simulation code.
actionItems: Review GPUPhysBench as a 50-task benchmark for agentic GPU physics simulation, with attention to the task mix across fluids, deformable solids, and granular materials and the correct-vs-efficient code objective.

Run comparative evaluations on the benchmark using write-compile-test-optimize loops under fixed time budgets, measuring pass rates and runtime against expert-optimized references, especially on collision detection, constraint solving, and iterative solvers.

Assess whether your current coding-agent workflow can reliably produce numerically accurate GPU simulation code that is also close to reference speed, given the reported efficiency gaps even when tasks are solved correctly.

papers.title: Neural Harmonic Measure Operator
papers.authors: Jinjin He, Sinan Wang, Yuchen Sun, Bo Zhu
papers.abstract: We introduce Neural Harmonic Measure Operator (NHMO), a neural solver for elliptic PDE problems on variable-shape domains. The harmonic measure of a domain is the boundary probability distribution that, integrated against any boundary data, returns the Dirichlet Laplace solution. It depends only on the geometry, not on the boundary data. NHMO parameterizes the density of this measure as a transformer-based boundary kernel supervised by Walk-on-Spheres exit samples, so one trained kernel handles different boundary values on a shape with no retraining. We extend it to Poisson via a classical decomposition, with an auxiliary network amortizing the source-induced correction and avoiding the singular volume quadrature that breaks direct evaluation. At inference, new boundary values and new sources both yield PDE solutions by re-integration against the fitted kernel and lift, with no retraining. NHMO improves over four prior baselines on the MCB-B 3D variable-shape Poisson benchmark across all five categories, and is competitive with major neural-operator baselines on a controlled 2D testbed.
takeaways: Introduces Neural Harmonic Measure Operator (NHMO), a neural solver for elliptic PDEs on variable-shape domains that learns a geometry-dependent harmonic-measure kernel so one trained model can handle different boundary values without retraining.

Method: parameterizes the boundary density with a transformer-based kernel supervised by Walk-on-Spheres exit samples, and extends to Poisson using a classical decomposition plus an auxiliary network for the source-induced correction.

Evidence and implication: NHMO improves over four prior baselines on the MCB-B 3D variable-shape Poisson benchmark across all five categories and is competitive on a controlled 2D testbed, enabling inference on new boundary values and sources by re-integration only.
actionItems: Review the NHMO architecture and training setup, focusing on how the transformer-based boundary kernel is supervised by Walk-on-Spheres exit samples and how the geometry-dependent measure is reused across boundary conditions.

Run a head-to-head benchmark or ablation on the MCB-B 3D variable-shape Poisson task and the controlled 2D testbed to verify the reported gains versus the four prior baselines and competitive performance versus neural-operator baselines.

Assess deployment risk by checking whether the no-retraining inference path remains reliable for new boundary values and new sources, especially given the reported low reproducibility and the need to avoid direct singular volume quadrature.

papers.title: CoSE-E: A Benchmark for Code-switched Speech Evaluation in Enterprise Settings
papers.authors: Shama Gupta, Hoang H Nguyen, Chelsea Huang, Lindsay Devon Brin, Fanny Riols
papers.abstract: Code-switching (CS), a seamless alternation between languages within a single utterance, remains a critical challenge in automatic speech recognition (ASR). While prior works focus on conversational CS-ASR, enterprise settings demand evaluation of operational impact beyond edit-distance errors: how code-switching transcription errors propagate to downstream voice agent task failures. In this work, we propose (1) a CS-ASR synthetic benchmark and multidimensional evaluation framework tailored to enterprise domains, (2) systematic evaluation of frontier ASR systems across 5 language pairs, (3) diagnostic analysis of the additional transcription errors that code-switching introduces across language pairs and models. We release COSE-E to support enterprise-focused CSASR evaluation for multilingual voice agents in enterprise deployment.
takeaways: Introduces CoSE-E, a synthetic benchmark and multidimensional evaluation framework for code-switched speech in enterprise settings, focused on operational impact rather than only edit-distance errors.
Evaluates frontier ASR systems across 5 language pairs and performs diagnostic analysis of how code-switching adds transcription errors across language pairs and models.
Provides a release intended to support enterprise-focused CS-ASR evaluation for multilingual voice agents by linking transcription errors to downstream task failures.
actionItems: Review CoSE-E’s benchmark design and multidimensional enterprise evaluation framework to confirm it matches your voice-agent use case and target language pairs.
Run a baseline evaluation on your own ASR stack using CoSE-E’s 5 language-pair setup, measuring both transcription errors and downstream task-failure impact.
Ask whether the synthetic enterprise benchmark and code-switching error patterns transfer to your production setting, especially for the specific language pairs and task flows you deploy.
